0.0.n: Here it refers to his parents’ household and its business.

0.1.n: Marks 実家 as what is described as a sushi shop.

0.2.n: 屋 identifies a shop or business selling the preceding item.

0.3.n: Links the description 実家が寿司屋 to the person 大友.

0.4.n: This is the speaker’s family name.

0.7.n: A polite greeting after an introduction, shortened here from よろしくお願いします.

1.0.n: Refers to the introduction he has just given.

1.1.n: Adds the sense that he mentioned this just now, too.

1.2.n: Past form of 言う, placed before 通り.

1.3.n: After a verb, 通り means in the same way as what that verb describes.

1.4.n: A casual, often masculine self-reference; the following 実家 is understood as his family home.

1.5.n: Refers to his parents’ home and the business they run.

1.6.n: Marks 実家 as the thing being described.

1.8.n: Connects the noun 寿司屋 to explanatory んです.

1.9.n: Short for の; presents the statement as background for what follows.

1.10.n: Makes the explanatory ending んです polite.

1.11.n: Here it gently leads into the next point rather than expressing a strong contrast.

2.0.n: Refers to the speaker’s family restaurant.

2.1.n: Links the restaurant to its signature menu item.

2.2.n: Literally a signboard; in 看板メニュー, it describes the dish a restaurant is known for.

2.3.n: Here it means a dish offered, not the whole menu.

2.4.n: Marks the signature dish as the topic.

2.6.n: A Japanese dish steamed in a small cup, often with assorted ingredients.

3.0.n: Before 手前, it indicates the nearest position.

3.1.n: Refers literally to the near side or foreground; the exact referent depends on the scene.

3.2.n: Casual form of だろう, used here for a forceful assertion or challenge.

3.3.n: A blunt way to address someone, common in rough banter but potentially rude.

3.5.n: Names the dish the speaker expects to take priority.

3.6.n: Marks sushi as the comparison point for the surprising choice of egg custard.

3.7.n: Repeats the unexpected signature dish in disbelief.

3.8.n: This is か + よ + って, not かよう: a surprised challenge followed by a quotation marker.

4.0.n: Signals a transition to the next part of his routine.

4.2.n: Part of the description of people whose families run sushi shops.

4.3.n: Marks 実家 as what is a sushi shop.

4.4.n: Completes the description that labels this category of relatable experiences.

4.5.n: The first half of あるある, a repeated expression for familiar situations people recognize.

4.6.n: The second half completes あるある; the two parts work as one expression.

4.7.n: Polite form of 言う; he announces the relatable observation he is about to share.

5.0.n: Combines with 寿司 to name sushi served on a conveyor belt.

5.1.n: In 回転寿司, this refers to the conveyor-belt restaurant style.

5.2.n: Marks the destination of 行く.

5.3.n: Past form of 行く; with ことがない, it describes an experience someone has never had.

5.4.n: Turns 行った into an experience that can be said to exist or not exist.

5.5.n: Marks 行ったこと as the experience that does not exist.

5.6.n: Negates the existence of the experience, giving 行ったことがない the sense of never having gone.

6.0.n: Points back to the claim about never visiting conveyor-belt sushi restaurants.

6.1.n: Casual slang used with で to emphasize that the claim is genuine.

6.2.n: Combines with マジ to make マジで, which emphasizes the following statement.

6.3.n: Here it refers to people in the same family-business situation, not everyone generally.

6.4.n: Adds another layer of emphasis to his claim.

6.5.n: Refers to never having visited a conveyor-belt sushi restaurant.

6.6.n: Connects そう to the explanatory ending の.

6.7.n: Ends an emphatic explanation here, rather than a question.

6.9.n: Repeats the slang emphasis to insist he truly has never gone.

6.10.n: Forms マジで with the preceding word.

6.11.n: Here 行った is the past form of 行く, not 行う.

6.12.n: Used in 行ったことない, with the subject particle が omitted in casual speech.

6.13.n: Denies having the experience of going there.

6.14.n: Adds emphatic explanation to the statement that he has never gone.

7.0.n: This is うち plus conversational さ, not a form of うつ.

7.2.n: Negative form of 回る; describes a restaurant without a sushi conveyor belt.

7.3.n: Modified by 回らない to distinguish a conventional restaurant from conveyor-belt sushi.

7.4.n: Plain form used before から to explain the reason.

7.5.n: Marks the preceding statement as his reason for never having gone.

7.7.n: Past form of 行く in the experience pattern 行ったことない.

7.8.n: Pairs with ない to express never having done something; が is omitted.

7.9.n: The destination is left unstated because the conveyor-belt restaurant is already understood.

8.0.n: Invites the listener’s attention or agreement before he continues.

8.2.n: Introduces his genuine feeling about visiting such a restaurant.

8.4.n: Repeats the word as he gathers momentum and emphasizes sincerity.

8.5.n: Adds a conversational appeal to the listener after 実際.

8.7.n: 行く in て-form + みる for trying something + たい for wanting to do it.

8.9.n: The て-form of 行く connects to みたい in the pattern for wanting to try an action.

8.10.n: Here it is みる + たい, not the separate expression みたい meaning looks like.

8.11.n: Makes the statement ending in たい polite.

8.12.n: Emphasizes his wish and presents it assertively to the listener.

0.lit: I am Otomo, whose family home is a sushi shop; please treat me kindly!
0.tip: The description before の identifies Otomo by his family’s business.

1.lit: As I also said just now, me, my family home is a sushi shop, but…
1.tip: なんですけど provides explanatory background and gently leads into the next point.

2.lit: As for our place’s signature menu item, it is savory steamed egg custard.
2.tip: 看板メニュー means a restaurant’s signature dish, not a menu printed on a signboard.

3.lit: It’s the very front, isn’t it, you! Egg custard rather than sushi, seriously, you’re saying!
3.tip: かよって splits into a surprised かよ and quotation marker って; it is not the verb かよう.

4.lit: Okay, I will tell a family-home-is-a-sushi-shop relatable experience.
4.tip: あるある names a familiar situation that people with shared experiences recognize.

5.lit: There is no experience of having gone to conveyor-belt sushi.
5.tip: Past verb + ことがない means someone has never had that experience.

6.lit: This, seriously, everyone really is like that! Seriously, there is no experience of having gone!
6.tip: Casual speech often drops が from 行ったことがない without changing the meaning.

7.lit: Our place, you know, because it is a non-rotating sushi shop, I have no experience of going.
7.tip: 回らない寿司屋 means a conventional sushi restaurant, contrasted with conveyor-belt sushi.

8.lit: You know, actually, actually, you know, I want to try going. I want to try going, I tell you!
8.tip: Verb in て-form + みたい means wanting to try doing something.
